questions.q: What does the probability ratio r_t(theta) equal when the current policy is identical to the policy that collected the data?
questions.explain: r_t(theta) = pi_theta(a_t|s_t) / pi_theta_old(a_t|s_t), which equals exactly 1 when theta has not changed from theta_old.

questions.q: For a positive advantage A_t, what happens once r_t(theta) exceeds 1 + epsilon?
options: The unclipped term is used because it's always preferred
The min() picks the clipped term, which caps the objective and removes incentive to keep increasing the ratio further
The advantage is set to zero
questions.explain: Once the ratio exceeds 1+epsilon, the clipped term (1+epsilon)*A_t is smaller than the unclipped r_t(theta)*A_t, so min() selects the clipped, smaller value, removing the incentive to push the ratio even higher.

questions.q: Why is the min() operation in the clipped surrogate objective described as 'pessimistic'?
options: It always selects the clipped value regardless of sign
It always picks the lower of the clipped and unclipped estimates, which can only remove incentive to over-update, never add to it
It sets the objective to negative infinity
It ignores the advantage estimate entirely
questions.explain: Taking the minimum of the two terms means the objective is a lower bound on the unconstrained surrogate — it never rewards pushing the ratio further once the trust region is exceeded.

questions.q: What are the two additional terms in the full PPO loss beyond the clipped policy objective?
options: A replay buffer penalty and a discount factor term
A value function loss (training the critic) and an entropy bonus (encouraging exploration)
A target network sync term and a Double DQN correction
questions.explain: The full PPO loss is L^CLIP minus c1 times the value function loss plus c2 times an entropy bonus, training the critic and discouraging premature convergence to a deterministic policy.

questions.q: Why is the probability ratio typically computed as exp(new_log_probs - old_log_probs) rather than dividing raw probabilities?
options: It is mathematically different and gives a different result
It is numerically more stable and matches how log-probabilities are already stored from rollout collection
It removes the need for an advantage estimate
It converts the ratio into a KL-divergence
questions.explain: exp(log(a) - log(b)) equals a/b mathematically, but computing it via the exponential of a log-difference is the standard, numerically stable approach, and log-probabilities are already what's stored from rollouts.
